description: BioSpace Systems is a project focused on developing innovative software for monitoring astronauts' health during space missions. Led by Cédric DJOHOZIN, a biomedical engineering graduate specializing in Biomedical and Hospital Maintenance, the project combines biomedical engineering, embedded systems, data analysis, and artificial intelligence.
summary: BioSpace is an offline health-monitoring copilot for astronauts on long missions, where contact with Earth is delayed or lost. It learns each astronaut's own baseline over 30 days, then flags deviations across 16 indicators in 7 physiological systems, explains every alert in plain language, tracks the follow-up action and escalates automatically to the medical team if nobody acts. It also produces a ready-to-send medical report (PDF and CSV) and includes an optional browser for public NASA OSDR human-spaceflight studies. On simulated missions it detected 7 of 7 anomaly scenarios, with 4.5 % of days showing a false alert on a nominal mission. Thresholds are illustrative and the data are synthetic or self-reported: BioSpace is a research prototype, not a medical device.
details:
The problem. On long-duration missions, communication with Earth is delayed or interrupted, so astronauts must notice many of their own health changes. A fixed population norm is a poor yardstick in spaceflight: what matters is how an astronaut deviates from their own normal.

What BioSpace does.

  • Personal baseline. The first 30 days set each indicator's mean and standard deviation.
  • 16 indicators, 7 systems: cardiovascular (resting heart rate, HRV, systolic pressure), bone and muscle, neuro-ocular (visual acuity, relevant to spaceflight-associated neuro-ocular syndrome), spine, blood and immunity, radiation (dose rate), and behaviour (sleep, mood, stress, social contact).
  • Detection. 7-day smoothing, a z-score corrected for the uncertainty of the baseline, oriented towards the dangerous direction of each indicator, and a persistence rule (3 consecutive days) so an isolated spike does not raise an alarm. Orange from 2.5, red from 4.0. Absolute safety thresholds (for example systolic pressure below 80 or above 160 mmHg, temperature above 38.5 °C) turn a system red immediately, even during calibration.
  • Explained alerts and action loop. Every alert states why it fired, which indicator drives it and what to do. Actions are tracked (to do, done, postponed, reported to the medical team); without action, the alert escalates automatically (1 day for red, 3 days for orange) and closes after 3 consecutive normal days.
  • Medical report. PDF and CSV exports are generated locally for the medical team.
  • Input. Guided daily check-in (about one minute, partial entries accepted) and validated CSV import.
  • Offline by design. Local SQLite storage, no telemetry. Only the optional NASA Data tab uses the network.

Measured, not claimed. A Validation tab runs simulated missions with random seeds distinct from the demo. With 40 missions per scenario: 4.5 % of days with an alert on a nominal mission (0.02 % red); 7 of 7 anomaly scenarios detected in every mission; median detection delays from 2 days (solar particle event) to 34 days (isolation), for deliberately slow 150-day drifts. The automated test suite (87 tests) and a code review caught and fixed two weaknesses: a perfectly regular baseline could disable an indicator, and low blood pressure was not monitored.

Tools and technologies. Python, Streamlit, pandas, NumPy, Plotly, SQLite, ReportLab, PyInstaller (standalone executable), pytest and GitHub Actions.

Limitations (stated openly). Thresholds are illustrative and not clinically validated. The detector runs on synthetic or self-reported data. The reference period is fixed at 30 days. BioSpace is not a medical device. Next steps: a physician-validated adaptive baseline, real wearable sensors, encrypted sync with the ground, and multi-crew support.

Use of AI (SI) tools. Generative AI assistants were used during development, and this is acknowledged here and in AI_USAGE.md in the repository. ChatGPT (OpenAI) helped draft and correct parts of the Python code, an initial NASA OSDR client, unit tests and documentation. Claude (Anthropic, through Claude Code) helped review the detection logic (two weaknesses found and fixed with regression tests), fix the NASA OSDR client against the real API, improve the interface performance and the PDF report layout, and draft the English submission texts and the 7-slide deck. The code and the claims were reviewed and tested by the team. No AI-generated images, video or audio are included.
